source.title: A Multi-resolution Theory for Approximating Infinite-p-Zero-n: Transitional Inference, Individualized Predictions, and a World Without Bias-Variance Tradeoff

page_placements.theme: Spectral learning stages and feature-inclusion order

record.tranche_reason: The paper develops theoretical and simulated prediction-error curves and argues that double or multiple descents can occur before over-parameterization, refining the usual account. It does not reproduce the original deep-network experiments.
record.gate_note: Rows cover the paper's own linear-model prediction-error curves and their stated conditions. Results cited from other work are excluded. Comparisons of CV, UE and IC as error estimators are not recorded unless the reported result describes the prediction-error curve itself.
record.test_reason: This is a theoretical and simulation study of linear least-squares prediction error as covariates are added (resolution r ≤ n−3, so never past interpolation). It bears on V6 because it derives, and simulates, how a rise toward r→n depends on intrinsic variance τ² and on how fast the unexplained 'pseudo-variance' A(r) decays. Its double and multiple descents (Figs 1–2) are built by ordering covariate importance non-monotonically, entirely inside the under-parameterized region. They are not the interpolation-threshold phenomenon any version names. It argues the mechanism may be more nuanced than over-parameterization, but it never measures risk past the interpolation point.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that with zero intrinsic variance the optimal resolution can approach n or infinity, i.e. traditional over-fitting. They argue this does not violate the bias-variance trade-off, which they call 'sound and well'. They also find that double and multiple descents can occur without over-parameterization, driven by varying resolution-bias decay versus estimation error. They suggest machine-learning double descent may be more nuanced than over-parameterization, offered as a hint rather than a demonstrated explanation for deep networks.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a multi-resolution theoretical framework, constructed linear-model examples, regression-tree theory, and linear-model simulations rather than the original deep-network experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curve behavior depends on intrinsic variance and on the decay pattern of resolution bias; the paper also distinguishes curves with exponential, polynomial and logarithmic bias decay.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction error can show double or arbitrarily many descents entirely within the under-parameterized region (r < n), with τ²=0. The pattern arises when covariates are added in an order misaligned with their predictive importance (Figs 1b, 2b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Non-monotone (multiple-descent) risk curves can arise below the interpolation threshold from inhomogeneous feature importance and inclusion order, without over-parameterization.

record.peer_reviewed: Journal of the American Statistical Association
record.problems: The direct curve examples are constructed theoretical linear-model settings, not deep networks. The figures do not provide extractable numerical curve values or uncertainty for those curves. The simulation uses n=50 and reports curve shapes in figures; it does not test epoch-wise or sample-size double descent.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the positive-variance Figure 3 conditions: the text says the six curve shapes are consistent with the theory but does not describe their individual shapes in extractable detail. The tables on CV, UE and IC estimator performance were omitted because those comparisons concern estimation methods, not additional measured double-descent outcomes.

untested.parts: All of it: no deep networks.
All of it: no training-time axis.
All of it: sample size is not swept at fixed r near the threshold (Fig A1 only shows the optimal r versus n).
All of it: r is capped at n−3, so risk past the interpolation point is never computed.
All of it: no single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location across axes.
Removal of the peak by optimally tuned regularization; label-noise-specific effects; multiple peaks tied to interpolation thresholds.
All of it: no replotting against an effective parameter count, although Section 5.1 argues raw p is a poor complexity index.

missing.what: Analytic result (Eq. 3.3, Section 3.1): with τ²>0 or constant explained variance, error explodes as r/n→1. With τ²=0, the 0/0 limit need not explode, depending on A(r) decay. This bears directly on the noise dependence of the peak.
τ²=0.5 simulations: true prediction-error curves rise sharply toward r=n−3. Oracle ropt is 4, 7, 6 for n=50 and 6, 17, 17 for n=200. This gives a noisy-condition contrast to r3–r5.

record.verdict_notes: Pure theory plus a linear-model simulation. The study never evaluates r > n−3, so it cannot speak to second descent past interpolation. The rows' V4 'challenges' labels are removed: an under-fitting-region descent does not contradict V4's past-interpolation claim. The V6 multiple-descent support is also removed, because the multiple descents are constructed via A(r) and are unrelated to interpolation thresholds. Published in JASA.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweeps and peaks near the size that just fits the training set.
Increasing sample size near an interpolation threshold and its effect on test error.
A general result across model classes, or a demonstration that risk descends after capacity passes the interpolation point.
Whether one measure of effective complexity predicts peak locations across model size, epochs and sample size.
Label-noise-specific effects and whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
Replotting against an effective parameter count and showing that the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: normal linear model with infinitely many covariates
rows.operation_detail: Theoretical prediction-error curve over resolution, with a constructed resolution-bias function; intrinsic variance τ²=0.
rows.value: figure only; text describes a double-descent curve occurring within the under-fitting region
rows.note: The authors attribute the curve to changing predictive importance of added covariates; they state the pattern occurs without entering the over-parameterized region.
rows.check: Descents occur at r < n = 100 and are driven by constructed covariate-importance ordering, not by an interpolation peak. V4 and V6 name the interpolation-threshold peak, so this row moves to fits_no_version. It is a theoretical curve (Eq. 3.3), not an empirical measurement.

rows.operation_detail: Theoretical prediction-error curve over resolution using a constructed resolution-bias function with repeating importance changes; intrinsic variance τ²=0.
rows.value: figure only; text describes a multiple-descent curve that does not die down at the end
rows.note: The paper says the non-decaying end is due to the constructed bias having interwoven exponential and polynomial decay.

rows.subject: normal linear model with infinitely many covariates
rows.operation_detail: Simulation prediction-error curve over resolution for exponential resolution-bias decay.
rows.value: figure only; the text states prediction error decreases monotonically with resolution
rows.note: This is a deterministic setting; the paper describes the error as decreasing monotonically rather than exhibiting a bias-variance trade-off.
rows.check: State relabelled. With τ²=0 and fast (exponential) bias decay, error falls monotonically up to r=47 with n=50: no rise near the threshold without variance. Table A3 gives ropt=47 and PE=1.90e-19. This is consistent with a noise-driven peak, so 'observed' fits V6 better than 'partial'.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 3(d), Appendix A9.3 final paragraph, Table A3: monotonically decreasing prediction error; oracle resolution 47 and prediction error 1.90 × 10⁻¹⁹.

rows.subject: normal linear model with infinitely many covariates

rows.value: figure only; text states the no-bias-variance-trade-off phenomenon did not occur for polynomial decay
rows.locator: Section 5.4; Appendix A9.3, Figure 3(e), Table A3
rows.note: The text does not specify a complete curve shape for this condition.
rows.check: With τ²=0 and polynomial decay, oracle ropt=23 < n−3 (Table A3), so error rises toward r→n even without intrinsic noise. The driver is unexplained variance A(r) from omitted covariates. The value should cite Table A3 rather than 'figure only'.

relationships.condition: Linear model, τ²=0, exponentially decaying resolution bias, n=50
relationships.reason: Without intrinsic or residual variance, error decreases monotonically to r=n−3, with no rise near the threshold (r3; Table A3, Theorem 3(ii)).
relationships.display_finding: Error decreased monotonically through resolution n−3, without rising near the threshold.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Linear model, τ²=0, exponentially decaying resolution bias, n=50
source_check.reason: The monotonic decrease through r=47 supports dependence on intrinsic variance and bias-decay rate. The supplied rationale needs correction: intrinsic variance is zero, but residual variance A(r)=e^(−r) is positive at finite r.

relationships.condition: Linear model, τ²=0, polynomial or logarithmic bias decay, n=50
relationships.reason: Error still rises toward r→n with zero label noise (ropt 23 and 12). The variance driving the peak can be omitted-feature bias, not noise (r4, r5).
relationships.display_finding: With zero label noise and n=50, error rose as r approached n despite optimal resolutions of 23 and 12 under the two bias-decay settings.

source_check.reason: Omitted-feature variance A(r) drives the large-resolution rise despite zero intrinsic noise. This supports V6's allowance for variance as a driver; it qualifies a stronger label-noise-necessity claim that V6 does not make.

relation.reason: Its own theoretical results and simulations bear on the variance-dependence component of V6.

tranche.reason: The paper explicitly argues that double and multiple descents need not require over-parameterization and derives how resolution-bias decay and intrinsic variance alter near-interpolation error behavior.

source_check.notes: The analyzed curves remain below interpolation; post-interpolation descent and optimally tuned regularization are untested. The polynomial and logarithmic expressions in Figure 3 describe decay rates; Appendix A9.2 specifies the finite-resolution coefficient constructions.

statements.correction: τ²=0; slowly decaying resolution bias leaves omitted-feature residual variance A(r)>0; prediction error rises at large tested resolutions; Table A3 oracle resolutions: polynomial 23, logarithmic 12, n=50. Intrinsic label noise is unnecessary; the variance explanation remains consistent with these results.
statements.problem: The factual description of this study is supported, but classifying it as against V6 overstates the implication: V6 permits variance, including variance from omitted features, as the driver.
